frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d368:
Charles Bohlen's minutes, the third set for 29 November 1943, record the dinner that evening at half past eight. They are less a record of decisions than of mood, and their most notable feature, Bohlen writes, was Stalin's manner toward Churchill.

Stalin kept a sharp edge on nearly every remark to the Prime Minister while staying entirely friendly. He teased him over Overlord. He implied a secret liking for the Germans and a wish for a soft peace. He spoke frankly of the Red Army's poor showing against Finland and its slow climb to a genuinely good army. On Germany he set two conditions: the physical liquidation of at least fifty thousand, perhaps a hundred thousand, of the German commanding staff, and Allied retention of the world's strong points. Roosevelt joked the figure down to forty-nine thousand; Churchill objected fiercely to cold-blooded execution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d468:

The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Leeper spoke for London to a restless exile government whose country was a battleground of resistance groups and rival claims. His reports to Eden fed British decisions about Greece at a moment when Cairo hosted both the exile court and the Allied conference. The message opens a window on the war's tangled Greek question.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d568:
Ambassador Averell Harriman recorded this memorandum on November 13, 1944, in Moscow. Harriman's memoranda often preserved his conversations and judgments about the Soviet leadership for the record in Washington. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By late 1944 Harriman's tone about Moscow was hardening: the cooperation promised at Tehran was meeting the facts of Soviet power in Poland and the Balkans. His written record from this season is a key source for the alliance's turn toward friction. For readers, the memorandum shows the ambassador setting down, carefully and on paper, what a year of dealing with Stalin's government had taught him.
frus-1944-quebec-d68:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this memorandum on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Second Quebec Conference. Stettinius remained in Washington while the leaders met in Canada. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

An opening-day memorandum from Washington shows the home government keeping pace with a traveling summit: positions restated, information supplied, and the department's interests guarded from a distance. Stettinius was also guarding the newborn United Nations project agreed at Dumbarton Oaks. For readers, the paper marks the State Department's parallel work while the conference ran.
frus-1944-quebec-d168:
An editors' note introduces the document printed next in the volume, the President's Log for the Quebec Conference. The Log was a booklet covering September 9 to 21, 1944, prepared by Lieutenant William Rigdon and approved by Rear Admiral Wilson Brown. The note describes its contents in detail, from the list of the president's party to the conference communiqué in an appendix.

The editors also compare the Log's party list with the one in Rigdon's later book, White House Sailor. Three names appear only in the book, and seven only in the Log, including Henry Morgenthau. Morgenthau's inclusion is explained: he accompanied Roosevelt from Washington to Hyde Park before being summoned to Quebec. The note is a small lesson in how the volume checks its own sources.
frus-1944-quebec-d268:
A draft directive to Admiral Mountbatten is proposed in C.C.S. 452/28, the British Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. His primary object would be the recapture of all Burma at the earliest date. That object must not prejudice the security of the air supply route to China, including the staging post at Myitkyina, whose protection was essential throughout.

Approved operations were the stages of Operation Capital needed for the air route, and Operation Dracula, the seaborne stroke at Rangoon. The chiefs attached the greatest importance to executing Dracula before the 1945 monsoon, with a target date of March 15. If it slipped past the monsoon, Capital would be exploited while Dracula was prepared for November 1945.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d68:

The note says the chapter gathers key documents showing where each main subject stood before the talks. Those subjects were the problems later discussed at Malta and Yalta, and each paper shows the position the United States had taken. The editors add that the military talks had a set agenda, while the political talks did not, and that fuller coverage would wait for later volumes.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d168:
Who really ran the armistice commissions in the Balkan capitals? This briefing book paper states the American position on the Allied Control Commissions in Rumania, Bulgaria, and Hungary. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The commissions mirror the Allied Commission in Italy, the paper explains, but with the leading role reversed: Russia leads, as Britain and America lead in Italy. Rumania's body works under rules drawn up by the Soviet government. Washington has not objected to Soviet officers running the day-to-day work while Germany still fights. But orders to local governments must not go out in the commission's name without prior word to the other members. Otherwise the United States is tied in public to acts it never saw.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d268:
Stalin surprised Churchill on war criminals at Moscow, and this excerpt of 22 October 1944 tells how. Paragraph five of message number 801 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet leader took what Churchill calls an unexpectedly ultra-respectable line.

There must be no executions without trial, Stalin held. Otherwise the world would say the allies were afraid to try the accused. Churchill pointed out the difficulties in international law. Stalin answered that if there were no trials, there must be no death sentences either, only lifelong confinement. Faced with that view from that quarter, Churchill tells Roosevelt, he will not press the memorandum he had given him. He asks that it be treated as withdrawn.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d368:

The three, he argued, could decide French participation themselves.

Then Ivan Maisky explained the Soviet reparations figures. Half would come at once, half in yearly payments. He set Germany's prewar national wealth at 125 billion, cut by war losses. Robert Ernest Hume, a Harvard Sanskritist, gathered the Thirteen Principal Upanishads into one English volume. Isa, Kena, Katha, and their companions appear with his notes and introductions. Generations of students learned Hindu philosophy from Hume's pages, and many still start there.

The Katha sends a boy to argue with Death about what survives the grave. The Chandogya teaches that the self and the world's ground are one: thou art that. Hume renders the Sanskrit with care for both sense and music. Verified from the 1919 public-domain edition, the volume remains the classic school text of the Upanishads in English.
podcast-joerogan-WZ1Dm-dcl68:
Journalist Amber Lyon joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 470. Lyon reported for CNN before leaving with sharp claims about how stories get steered and killed. Her visit is an exposé of media manipulation from a person who worked inside a major newsroom.

She tells Rogan what she saw: sponsors shaping coverage, war stories softened, and her own reporting on protest movements spiked. Rogan asks why more reporters do not speak. The episode is a young show's early statement of a theme it never dropped, that the news is a product, told here by a defector from the factory floor.
welsh-triads-skene-1868:
Welsh lore was kept in threes: three names, three deeds, three fates bound in one short saying. Trioedd Ynys Prydein, the Welsh Triads, gathers hundreds of these brief groups. Two Victorian versions stand here, William Skene's of 1868 and the Rhys and Evans text of 1887.

The triads name heroes, battles, bards, and wonders of old Britain in terse, packed lines. Bards used them as hooks on which long tales and poems could hang in memory. Read in bulk, they map the whole world of Welsh legend. The paired translations let readers test one rendering against the other.
brasseur-quatre-lettres-mexique-1868:
Charles-Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg spent years in Mexico and Central America copying old books and ruins. Quatre lettres sur le Mexique, printed in French in 1868, states his bold link between the Maya and Atlantis. Brasseur was the great Mayanist of his century, finder of lost texts.

In four letters he reads Maya myth, script, and ruin as signs of an Atlantic mother land. The letters show a pioneer scholar thinking aloud, half in proof and half in dream. Later writers on Maya and Atlantis all had to pass his work. The book is the founding statement of the Maya-Atlantis tie.
brinton-myths-of-new-world-1868:
Daniel Brinton, an American student of Native peoples, answered the lost-land school head-on in 1868. The Myths of the New World argues that like myths grow on their own in far lands. Brinton was a trained doctor turned scholar of tongues and lore.

He reads the myths of the Americas as the work of minds much like our own, facing the same sky and fears. No sunken land, he holds, is needed to explain why tales rhyme across oceans. Atlantis writers after him had to deal with his case or look weak. The book is the great skeptical counterweight of its age.
condon-report-1968:
The United States Air Force paid for a full science study of UFOs, and the study closed the file in 1968. The Condon Report, made at the University of Colorado under Edward Condon, is that study in full. Its word was blunt: more study of UFOs was not worth the cost.

Teams weighed sightings, photos, and physical traces case by case for two years. The report found no proof that the things seen came from past the earth, and much proof of error and hoax. On its word the Air Force shut Project Blue Book in 1969. No paper in the UFO file has weighed more since.
ufo-symposium-house-1968:
Scientists took the UFO question to a House panel in the summer of 1968. The Symposium on Unidentified Flying Objects, held July 29 by the Committee on Science and Astronautics, prints their talks in full. Allen Hynek, Carl Sagan, and James McDonald stood among the speakers.

The men split: some held the reports hid a true wonder worth a hunt, others saw error and noise. Leo Sprinkle and James Harder added their own cases and claims. The talks form the science counterpoint to the Condon study of the same year. The file shows the UFO fight argued at its highest level.
nsa-ufo-hypothesis-1968:
Analysts at the National Security Agency weighed what UFOs might mean for human survival in 1968. UFO Hypothesis and Survival Questions sets out five hypotheses for the things seen in the sky. The paper is laid to Lambros Callimahos, a famed code man of the agency.

Each hypothesis is tried for what it would ask of mankind if it proved true. The close is a fable, the Tale of the Rattler, on how pride can blind a mind to a new fact. The monograph is philosophy from inside the most sealed of agencies. It shows cleared men wondering aloud at their own desks.
smyth-antiquity-intellectual-man-1868:
C. Piazzi Smyth argued that man is far more old than most held in On the Antiquity of Intellectual Man, out in 1868. Smyth was a star chief who read dates in stone and sky. He draws on ice ages, star shifts, and the dates writ in the Great Pyramid to push man's dawn far back in time.

His case lands in the midst of the row sparked by Darwin. Church and lab men both felt its force. Smyth holds faith and deep time can stand as one. The book shows his stone school at its most bold.
redi-generation-of-insects-1668:
Francesco Redi, doctor to the dukes of Tuscany, ran these famed trials on the birth of insects in 1668. The text here is the 1909 English version by Mab Bigelow. In Redi's day most men held that maggots were born from rot itself.

Redi set meat in jars, some open, some sealed, and some veiled with fine gauze. Flies laid eggs on the gauze, and no maggots grew in the sealed jars at all. The clean result struck the first strict blow at the claim that life springs from rot. His method of matched jars is still taught to young students.
broca-eyzies-1868:
Paul Broca, a French surgeon and sage of the brain, wrote this memoir on the Eyzies finds in 1868. The text here is the English version of his report. Work men in the Perigord had found five frames in a rock shelter that year.

The frames were the first Cro-Magnon men known to science, tall and fine boned. Broca set out their skulls and bones with care and told how they stand to living races. The paper is the first learned word on the Cro-Magnon folk, our own kind in the ice age.
nilsson-primitive-inhabitants-scandinavi:
Sven Nilsson, a Swedish sage of beasts and old times, wrote this classic on the first folk of Scandinavia. John Lubbock turned it into English in 1868. Nilsson had long taught that the north had its own stone age, rich with finds.

He sets out the stone tools, shell heaps, and graves of the first north men. He matches them with the ways of wild folk of his own day to guess their life. The book is the north's match to the French case for deep age man, and a classic of its kind.
grosh-oddfellows-manual-1868:
Aaron B. Grosh was a clergyman and a leading Odd Fellow in the United States. His Odd-Fellow's Improved Manual came out in 1868. It set out the past, the rules, and the aims of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. The order was then one of the largest friendly groups in the land.

Grosh defends the order against its critics and explains its signs, degrees, and lodge work. He also gives the laws that govern local lodges and grand lodges. For the years when such groups cared for the sick and buried the dead, few books show their inner life so well.
skene-four-ancient-books-wales-vol-2-186:
William F. Skene was a Scots sage of the Celts and their past. His Four Ancient Books of Wales came out in two books in 1868. Book Two holds the texts and their English dress. The four books are old Welsh tomes with poems from the dark age of Britain.

Poems tied to Taliesin, Aneirin, and the bards of the old north fill the text. Gods, kings, and wars of the Britons crowd the wild verse. Skene prints the Welsh text with his dress at hand for the reader. The set is a chief source for the first verse of Wales.
sterne-sentimental-journey-1768:
Laurence Sterne published A Sentimental Journey, his tour of France and Italy, in 1768, his last work in print. The unfinished travel narrative named sensibility and founded sentimental travel literature in the English tradition of prose. Sterne died weeks after its first volumes charmed London readers with Yorick's gentle, wandering heart abroad.

Parson Yorick drifts from Calais to Paris, collecting small scenes of feeling over sights and facts. A monk refused alms, a caged starling, and a peasant's dead ass become tests of his heart. He flirts, weeps, and moralizes by turns, and the journey breaks off mid-sentence at his death. The book taught Europe to value the traveler's inner weather over maps, miles, and monuments en route. Its influence runs through travel writing and the novel of feeling for a hundred years.
dilke-greater-britain-1868:
Charles Dilke was a young British writer and member of Parliament who traveled around the English-speaking world in the 1860s. His 1868 book Greater Britain reports that trip through America, Australia, and India. He was only in his twenties when the trip made his name. It was a bestseller in its day.

Dilke described how English speech, law, and habits were spreading across whole continents. He asked what that spread meant for the future power of Britain and the United States. The book gave a name and a shape to the idea of a worldwide English-speaking family of nations.
darwin-variation-vol-1-1868:
After the Origin of Species, Darwin set out to print the mass of facts behind his theory. The first volume of The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication appeared in 1868. It surveys bred animals, from pigeons and dogs to horses and cattle.

Darwin records how breeders pick traits, how traits pass to the young, and how strange forms appear without plan. He moves through poultry, rabbits, fruit trees, and grain in dense, careful detail. Pigeons get special care, since their many breeds showed Darwin how far selection could go. Breeders and biologists mined the volume for years as a storehouse of evidence.
darwin-variation-vol-2-1868:
The second volume of Darwin's Variation, also published in 1868, turns from facts to causes. Having listed how bred animals and plants change, Darwin asks why those changes happen and how they pass on. It is the more daring half of the work.

Here he sets out pangenesis, his guess that tiny particles from every part of the body gather in the seed. Later science dropped that guess, but the questions he framed drove the study of inheritance for decades. The volume closes his case that selection, by man or nature, explains the forms of life.
dryden-essay-dramatic-poesy-1668:
John Dryden published An Essay of Dramatic Poesy in 1668, just after the London theaters reopened following plague and fire. Dryden was already England's leading playwright and critic. The essay takes the form of a conversation among four friends.

The friends drift in a boat on the Thames while a naval battle sounds in the distance. They debate whether ancient or modern writers are better, and whether French order or English variety makes stronger plays. Dryden gives each side its best case before siding, mostly, with the English. The essay is graceful, balanced, and often called the first real work of English literary criticism.
nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-1868:
Henry Callaway published Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus in 1868. Callaway, an English missionary and later bishop in Natal, took the tales down in the Zulus' own words. He prints the Zulu text with English translation and notes, so readers meet the storytellers' phrasing, not a summary.

Tricksters, ogres, and clever children fill the nursery tales, while the traditions recount chiefs and migrations. The histories preserve how Zulu elders of that generation told their own past. Callaway's method was new: record first, interpret with care, and credit the speakers. His volume became the founding English collection of Zulu oral literature. Folklorists still build on the texts he saved from vanishing.
plos-pone-0003368:
Xi-Song Ke, Yi Qu, Naomi Goldfinger and colleagues induce a cell transition in prostate cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Epithelial to mesenchymal transition, or EMT, has been connected with cancer progression in vivo and generation of more aggressive cancer cell lines in vitro. EMT has been induced in prostate cancer cell lines, but had previously not been shown in primary prostate cells.

The authors report EMT of a primary prostate cell line with switches of cell adhesion modules but without malignant transformation, as the title states. Readers learn the transition alone does not make cells cancerous. Separating shape change from malignancy refines how EMT is used as a cancer warning sign.
plos-pone-0003468:
Tristan H. Coady and co-authors built a gene therapy tool for a muscle disease in this 2008 paper. Spinal muscular atrophy comes from losing a gene called SMN1. A near-twin gene, SMN2, remains but its RNA is spliced wrongly. RNA tools that redirect splicing offer a possible fix.

Their single vector system boosted a method called trans-splicing of SMN2 messages. Better efficiency matters as such tools move toward patient use. One vector is simpler to deliver than several parts. The work moves RNA repair for this disease a step forward. The disease strikes infants, which makes each step toward treatment urgent.
plos-pone-0003568:
Alexander Karnowski and co-authors studied gene silencing in young B cells in this 2008 paper. B cells mature in stages toward making antibodies. At the pre-B stage, one gene locus, λ5, must be switched off. Switching off also involves moving the locus within the nucleus.

Two factors, Aiolos and OBF-1, were each implicated in B cell growth. Mice lacking either one developed early B cells largely normally. Together, the two proved required for silencing and repositioning λ5. Developing B cells thus lock away genes they have outgrown. B cells that fail these steps can leave the body short of antibodies.
plos-pone-0003668:
Tohshin Go and Yukuo Konishi published this newborn study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Healthy babies copy an adult's mouth movements within hours of birth. This oral imitation fades by about two to three months, as higher brain control grows.

The authors tested newborns with severe brain damage to see if the copying still appears. Whether it does can hint at which brain parts the reflex needs. The study uses a simple behavior to probe the workings of the injured newborn brain, where direct tests are hard to run. Few studies can test such questions in newborns at all.
plos-pone-0003768:
Armando Bartolazzi, Calogero D'Alessandria, Maria Gemma Parisella, and colleagues published this imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Thyroid nodules are common, and about ninety percent of them are benign. Telling harmless lumps from cancer before surgery is a standing problem. The team targeted galectin-3, a protein that helps cells avoid death.

They used that target to image thyroid cancer in living patients. Because galectin-3 marks malignant tissue, scans could flag the dangerous nodules. The approach could spare many patients needless surgery on growths that would never harm them. Better triage before surgery is the prize the authors aim at.
plos-pone-0003868:
Janet Mann, Brooke L. Sargeant, Jana J. Watson-Capps, and colleagues published this animal behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Some bottlenose dolphins carry sea sponges on their beaks while foraging. Tool use is rare in wild animals and prized as a window on cognition, social learning, and culture. Its costs and benefits are hard to measure.

The authors quantified what sponge carrying gains dolphins and what it costs them. Because nearly a whole population can be compared, spongers and non-spongers offer a rare natural test. The analysis weighs tool use the way evolution would: payoff against effort.
plos-pone-0003968:
Warunee Dansithong, Cordula M. Wolf, Partha Sarkar, and co-authors tested a proposed cause of myotonic dystrophy in 2008. Type 1 myotonic dystrophy comes from an expanded CTG tract in one gene. The mutant RNA forms clumps, called foci, in cell cytoplasm. Those clumps were thought to drive much of the disease.

Their PLOS ONE article reports the foci alone are not enough. Key features of the disease failed to appear from foci by themselves. Heart involvement in the disease also centers on the mutant RNA. The result pushes the field to find what else the expansion does.
plos-pone-0004068:
Saori Morino, Tatsuya Kondo, Kazunari Sasaki, and co-authors tested mild electric stimulation in diabetes models in 2008. Mild electrical stimulation can activate the PI3K and Akt signal path. Insulin resistance involves marked failure of that same path. Heat shock proteins also help cells handle stress.

Their PLOS ONE article combined mild stimulation with heat shock treatment. The pairing improved insulin resistance through stronger insulin signaling. A physical treatment that restores signaling would differ from drug therapy. The result invites tests of device-based help for type 2 diabetes. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004168:
Nathan Georgette published this modelling study in PLOS ONE in 2009. During an outbreak, officials need to know how much vaccination is enough to stop spread. The target is the coverage level that brings the average number of new infections per case below one.

Georgette built a new algorithm, a step-by-step computing method, that predicts this threshold from field survey data gathered while an outbreak unfolds. He calls the target the Outbreak Response Immunization Threshold. A tool that updates the target as real data arrive could help teams vaccinate enough people without wasting scarce doses.
plos-pone-0004268:
Marcela Guzman-Ayala and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The TGF-beta signalling family includes morphogens such as Nodal and Activin, signals that guide vertebrate development. The concentration of a morphogen is critical: cells read the dose to decide their fate. Smad2 and Smad3 carry those signals inside the cell.

Using embryonic stem cells, the team asked how graded activation of Smad2 and Smad3 translates into gene activity. They report that the graded signal is converted directly into levels of target gene expression. Dose in, dose out: the study shows a simple arithmetic at the heart of development.
plos-pone-0004368:
Katherine Hammond and colleagues published this zebrafish ear study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bone morphogenetic protein genes bmp2 and bmp4 are expressed in highly conserved patterns in the developing vertebrate inner ear. Elucidating BMP function during ear development has proved difficult, because mutations in these genes cause early embryonic defects that mask later roles.

The team focused on a late role for bmp2b in the morphogenesis of semicircular canal ducts in the zebrafish inner ear. Those canals sense head rotation and balance. Finding what builds them, stage by stage, informs the biology of balance disorders.
plos-pone-0004468: In 2009, Singh, Mohan, and Isaac found prions moonlighting in iron trade. Prion protein modulated cellular iron uptake directly. The infamous protein ran a quiet normal iron job. The finding links prions to brain iron balance. The iron function is entirely novel.
plos-pone-0004568: In 2009, Roy warned that copied genes fool family trees quite badly. Gene duplication and hidden unrecognized paralogy distorted phylogenomics. The lost gene copies misled outgroup choice quite badly. The neat paper sharpens tree building practice today. Gene duplication is common.
plos-pone-0004668: In 2009, Kijas, Townley, and Dalrymple read sheep breeds' genetic blueprints anew. A genome-wide survey of SNP variation revealed the genetic structure of sheep breeds. The domestication history emerged clearly. The work aids breeding programs. The breed structure guides genetics.
plos-pone-0004768: In 2009, a team caught monkey moms overdoing tool use for babies anew. Free-ranging macaque mothers exaggerated tool-using behavior when watched by offspring. The moms performed for the young proudly. The study maps cultural transmission patterns. The use is group-wide.
stowe-men-of-our-times-1868:
Stowe gathered short lives of leading men in Men of Our Times, printed at Hartford in 1868. The title page lists Lincoln, Grant, Garrison, Sumner, Chase, and Greeley among its subjects. Eighteen steel portraits illustrate the book, which was sold by subscription only.

Generals, statesmen, and orators of the Civil War years fill the pages, from Farragut and Sherman to Douglass and Beecher. Stowe wrote for young readers and aimed to teach character as much as history. Each sketch asks what made its man great and what boys might learn from him. The volume shows Stowe the moral teacher at work.
npt-1968:
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signing in 1968, after years of fear that atomic weapons would spread to many nations. It rests on a bargain between the states that already had nuclear arms and those that did not. Nearly every country in the world has since joined, making it the widest arms control agreement in force.

States without nuclear weapons promise never to build or receive them, and they accept inspections of their atomic programs. The nuclear powers promise to work toward disarmament and to share peaceful nuclear technology. The bargain has kept the circle of nuclear-armed states small for over fifty years, even as disputes over disarmament and enforcement continue to test it.
cia-0000007468:
Volume 6, number 2 of Studies in Intelligence appeared in spring 1962, inside the CIA's own publishing program. Studies was the agency's in-house journal, written by officers for officers about their craft. The issue's heading names a piece on Die Piratenchronik, a chronicle tied to pirates.

Because the journal was meant for internal readers, its pages speak more plainly than public statements do. Articles in the series weigh sources, methods, and past operations for lessons. Historians now use these issues to trace how American intelligence thought during the Cold War. The declassified copy comes through the CIA reading room mirror.
cia-0000009668:
The location of an American prisoner of war camp in Bac Thai province, current as of November, is fixed in a February 1970 item. Bac Thai, north of Hanoi, held camps close to the capital's prison system. A dated location mattered because camps moved and reports aged fast.

Pinpointing a camp served several needs: rescue planning, bombing safety, and the prisoner accounting itself. Analysts had to state how fresh the fix was, hence the November dating. Stale locations could mislead as badly as none. This short item shows the care taken to keep the prison map current month by month.
cia-0000009968:
France's current situation, including its strategic importance, fills a CIA paper dated November 1947. France was then governed by shifting coalitions, with the largest communist party in Western Europe newly expelled from government. Strikes shook the country that same autumn.

The paper reads France as a Cold War hinge: lose France, and Western Europe's defense crumbled. That reading drove aid, diplomacy, and quiet political support for the center. Coming months after the CIA's founding, the file shows the agency thinking continent-wide from birth. It also preserves French weakness, before recovery, as Washington plainly saw it.
cia-0000010668:
Six years after Japan's defeat, CIA analysts asked a hard question in March 1951: could Japan rebuild armed forces while working with the United States? Japan was still under American occupation, and its new constitution barred it from keeping an army. The Korean War, raging next door, made the question urgent for planners in Washington.

The study weighs what rearmament would take in men, money, and public support. It also considers how Japan's neighbors would react to a rearmed former enemy. The paper came months before the peace treaty was signed, and it foreshadows the Self-Defense Forces Japan created soon after.
cia-0000012268:
A letter meant for the appropriate authorities of the United States sits in the CIA files from June 1960. The document's spare title hides its errand: it is part of the routing around the Penkovsky operation. Oleg Penkovsky, a Soviet intelligence colonel, was reaching toward the West with offers of secrets that summer.

The file preserves how his mail was handled once it entered American hands. Cover sheets, routing marks, and careful logging guarded each step of the journey. For readers, it is postal history from the Cold War's greatest espionage case, plain on its face and grave in its stakes.
cia-0000013868: How American prisoners of war were treated is the subject of a CIA report dated July 4, 1967. Treatment covered food, care, housing, and the rules guards were told to follow. Reports like this reached officials who had to judge camp life in North Vietnam and the south. They also shaped what the public was told about the prisoners.
cia-0000014668: An admitted Soviet agent gave testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, in a CIA file dated February 1, 1966. The agent's name is left blank in the title line. Such testimony fueled public spy scares through the 1950s and beyond. The file keeps the hearing in the agency's long watch on Soviet work in America.
cia-0000014768: Birthday greetings for Togliatti sit beside Rosenberg clemency in a CIA file dated February 5, 1953. Palmiro Togliatti led Italy's huge Communist Party. Trieste's Communists looked to Rome as much as to Moscow. Pairing a party feast day with the mercy campaign shows the human weave of these small party reports. This party file is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015268: An unexplained bright light traveled across the sky, in a CIA file dated September 1, 1958. The title gives no place, only the moving light itself. cia-0000015368: Comments on a sighting report fill a CIA file dated May 1, 1954. The report is coded OO-B-90229, a sighting of unconventional aircraft. The source date is marked unknown in the title. cia-0000015468: Above a Norwegian town, an unidentified object was seen, and a CIA record dated in 1952 kept the report. The title names neither the town nor the witness, so no detail is added here. Small place sightings formed the bulk of the saucer file in every country. Each one was minor alone, yet together they built the pile officials felt bound to track.
cia-0000022168: Israel's situation after its war with the Arab states is discussed in a CIA record dated in 1968. The war meant is the June 1967 war, which redrew the map of the region. A year on, officials were still taking stock of borders, armies, and talks. The clipped title frames the item as Israel discussing its own state, a view worth keeping.
cia-0000022368: Finns demanded to know why Powers had orders to land on a Finnish airfield, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. Emergency landing orders in his papers named fields in neutral Finland. That detail pulled a careful neutral country into a spy scandal. The demand shows small states guarding their good name when great powers fly secret missions overhead.

A CIA Latin America brief for November 21, 1989 is dated October 2, 1989 in the catalog record. Parts of the brief are blanked out in the released copy. Its El Salvador item says the country faced human rights concerns.

Inside, the brief gives the region's news in short, ranked form. El Salvador's rights record was then under sharp attack at home and abroad. Congress in Washington weighed the charges each time new military aid came up for a vote. The file shows a daily brief doing its plain work. It placed one country's troubles on the morning page, where officials in Washington began their reading of the region each day.
cia-0000046768: CIA analysts looked ahead at Eastern Germany's likely course through 1952 in an estimate dated January 2, 1952. East Germany was then a new state, built in the Soviet zone of the defeated country. Forecast papers like this one show planners trying to read a satellite's politics month by month. Most such guesses were soon tested by events.
cia-0000049168: An update on progress in the Jesuit murder case is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Updates like this one were the case's pulse, taken for readers in San Salvador and Washington. Each reported a step, a stall, or a name, in a case that took years to reach a courtroom.
cia-0000049268: The 1990 certification of El Salvador fills a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. Each round forced the war's record into a yes-or-no shape, and this file holds one round's paper.

In that group, the test proved surprisingly specific: positive results truly pointed to M. tuberculosis infection. Timing, it seems, is part of the test's meaning. Close contacts of TB cases are the very people health workers most need to sort. A cheap skin test that can be trusted in that setting is valuable for clinics with few resources.
plos-pone-0000168:
Mark B. Bain, Nancy Haley, Douglas L. Peterson, and colleagues published this fisheries paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reports the recovery of an endangered fish in the United States. Once in steep decline, the species had rebounded enough to stand as a conservation success.

Recovery stories are rare enough to be worth documenting in detail. The authors lay out the evidence for the rebound and the conditions behind it. Their account gives managers a worked example of what a fish recovery looks like, useful when other endangered species need a path back.
plos-pone-0000268:
Honglin Song, Susan J. Ramus, Susanne Krüger Kjaer, and colleagues published this cancer genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests whether tagging single nucleotide polymorphisms, common one-letter DNA variants, in the BRIP1 gene relate to susceptibility to breast and ovarian cancer. BRIP1 works in DNA repair and partners with the famous BRCA1 gene.

Faulty DNA repair is a known route to these cancers, so repair genes are natural suspects. The authors genotype the variants in patients and controls to test the link. Association studies of this kind sort which inherited variants genuinely shift cancer risk and which are innocent bystanders.
plos-pone-0000368:
Beth Burgwyn Fuchs, Robin J. Tang, and Eleftherios Mylonakis studied a disease-causing fungus, Cryptococcus neoformans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The fungus can cause serious illness in people with weak immune systems. Their work focuses on a gene called ROM2 and on how it shapes the fungus's cells, with special attention to the role of temperature.

Cell shape in fungi is tied to growth, survival, and the ability to cause disease. A gene whose effect changes with temperature is of special interest because the fungus must adapt to the warmth of the human body. Understanding how ROM2 guides cell building helps explain how this fungus copes with its host.
plos-pone-0000468:
Yonatan Savir and Tsvi Tlusty proposed a way that molecules double-check their partners, in a 2007 PLOS ONE theory paper. Molecular recognition must be specific: a protein should bind its true partner and reject near-matches. The authors describe conformational proofreading, in which a molecule's change of shape on binding adds a check that improves specificity.

The idea extends the classic proofreading concept from DNA copying to shape-shifting molecules generally. A flexible molecule pays an energy cost when it molds to a partner, and the wrong partner makes that cost higher. Theory of this kind gives experimentalists a sharper question: how much of a molecule's selectivity comes from its willingness to change shape?
plos-pone-0000568:
Andrey O. Kiselev and colleagues followed one chlamydia protein through the germ's life cycle, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Chlamydia trachomatis causes a common infection passed by sex, and can blind in its trachoma form. The team tracked the protein PmpD: when it is made, how it is trimmed, and where it sits in the cell.

This germ swaps between a hardy spread form and a growing form inside cells. Each stage wears a different set of proteins. A protein's timing and place hint at its job, be it entry, growth, or exit. Proteins tracked this closely become vaccine leads for an infection that often does harm before it is noticed.
plos-pone-0000668:
Supriya Srinivasan, Pamela Santiago, Cecile Lubrano and co-authors retooled a cell receptor so its signals could be turned up or down in live animals. Their 2007 PLOS ONE target was the melanocortin-4 receptor. It belongs to a large family of receptors that sit in cell membranes and pass signals inward. That family runs many body processes, from hunger to hormone release.

The hard part is proof: with so many receptors at work, which signal causes which body response? By building a receptor they could control, the team could switch its signals on at will. That covered both its steady activity and the activity sparked by a binding molecule. The melanocortin-4 receptor is known for its role in appetite and weight, so a controllable version is a sharp tool for that field.
plos-pone-0000768:
Lars Palmqvist, Nicolas Pineault, Carina Wasslavik and colleagues hunted for genes that let fusion proteins expand blood stem cells. Hox genes help regulate hematopoietic stem cells and are also implicated in leukemia, through fusions with the nucleoporin gene NUP98. An engineered NUP98-HOXA10 fusion can expand these stem cells several hundred-fold in vitro, a striking and useful effect.

The team sought candidate genes behind that expansion and the transformation toward leukemia. Knowing which downstream genes do the work could separate the welcome expansion from the dangerous transformation. Stem cell expansion is a prize for transplantation medicine, where too few cells limit treatment. Leukemia risk is the shadow that comes with it.
plos-pone-0000868:
Amro Zayed, Serban Constantin and Laurence Packer studied an invading species that thrived despite a heavy genetic load, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Invasions can do real harm to local wildlife and to farming. Oddly, invading groups often show little loss of genetic variety, even when they start from few founders.

The authors take up a case where the genetic burden was severe, yet the invasion still worked. That puzzle tests simple ideas about why some introductions fail and others spread. Their work speaks to anyone trying to predict which new arrivals will take hold. It also shows that genes alone do not settle the outcome.
plos-pone-0000968:
Niyaz Ahmed, Vikram Saini, Saurabh Raghuvanshi and colleagues analyzed a bacillus used in leprosy immune therapy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mycobacteria include both germs that cause disease and harmless soil dwellers. How they split into those paths is a question of evolution, driven by how they colonize hosts and spread.

The team read the bacillus at the molecular level to place it among its relatives. A therapy strain needs a clear identity before its effects can be judged. Their analysis also feeds the wider story of mycobacterium evolution. Knowing which traits came with host living helps explain why some relatives cause leprosy or tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0001068:
Tali Sharot, Mieke Verfaellie and Andrew Yonelinas examined how emotion makes memories feel vividly recollected, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Emotion strengthens the subjective sense of remembering, even when the memory is no more accurate than a plain one. That gap between feeling and fact is a known trap in eyewitness settings.

The authors test whether the effect runs through hippocampal memory consolidation over time. They lay out two critical predictions of that idea and test them. A time dependent hippocampal process would mean the vividness grows as the memory settles. The work helps separate the feeling of certainty from the evidence behind it.
plos-pone-0001168:
In 2005 and 2006, the island of La Réunion in the Indian Ocean suffered a large outbreak of chikungunya, a fever spread by mosquitoes. Marie Vazeille and colleagues studied the outbreak's virus in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mosquito blamed was Aedes albopictus, the Asian tiger mosquito.

The authors present the first study of how local mosquito populations responded to virus isolates taken from the same outbreak. Two isolates showed different patterns of infection in the mosquito. Differences like these can help explain why an outbreak explodes in one place and fizzles in another.
plos-pone-0001268:
Violence fills much media fare, and claims that it breeds aggression are old. Christopher Kelly, Jack Grinband, and Joy Hirsch looked for effects in the brain networks that control behavior, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, they studied repeated exposure to media violence.

The authors report a diminished response in an inhibitory frontolimbic network after repeated exposure to violent media. Just as thrilling nonviolent media did not produce it. That network usually helps restrain impulses. Their finding gives the media violence debate a measurable brain correlate to argue over.
plos-pone-0001368:
Kui Yang and colleagues reported work in PLOS ONE in 2007 on a fast way to read fats in cell walls. These fats, called ether lipids, are common in the heart and brain. They help cells work well. Shifts in their mix have been tied to a number of gene based ills.

By blasting samples and reading the mass of each fat, the team found a paired rule. The rule links which forms of these fats show up side by side. A clear rule like this can speed up lab work. It can also help track how fat levels shift in health and in disease.
plos-pone-0001468:
Gilles Charvin, Frederick Cross, and Eric Siggia published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on watching yeast cells grow over many cycles. Films of single cells with glow markers are a strong tool for cell cycle work. Tiny fluid devices now let labs control the cell's world with care. The team built one such device for yeast.

Their device lets them switch genes on at set times and film cells for days. The cells divide in a calm, unstressed way in the device. That calm is key, since stress can fake or hide gene effects. The tool should serve any lab that tracks slow cell change live.
plos-pone-0001568:
Bob Uttl wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE review on memory for future acts and aging. This kind of memory is the knack of recalling a plan at the right time and place. After two decades of work, reviews had reached clashing verdicts on whether age harms it. Uttl pooled the past studies in an open, checkable way.

His pooled read sorts lab tests from real world tests, which give unlike answers. That split may explain much of the clash in the field. A clear verdict guides how older adults can be aided with cues and tools. It also sets the bar for future aging and memory work.
plos-pone-0001668:
Jane F. Fearnside, Marc-Emmanuel Dumas, Alice R. Rothwell, and their co-authors compared mouse strains on a high-fat diet in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Insulin resistance, in which tissues stop responding well to insulin, sits at the center of type 2 diabetes and obesity. Both genes and environment shape it. Inbred mice fed a high-fat diet develop insulin resistance, making them a useful test system.

The team used phylometabonomics, a method that combines family history of strains with chemical profiles of their bodies. The full text gives the strain comparisons, the chemical patterns, and which strains adapted well or badly to the diet. Matching chemical profiles to strain ancestry helps predict which animals, and by extension which people, are most at risk from a fatty diet.
plos-pone-0001768:
Gesa Feenders, Miriam Liedvogel, Miriam Rivas, and their co-authors mapped movement areas in bird brains in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Vocal learning, the ability to imitate sounds, underlies human spoken language. It is rare, found in three distant bird groups: songbirds, hummingbirds, and parrots. Those groups share strikingly similar systems of cerebral vocal nuclei for learning and producing sounds.

The team mapped movement-associated areas in the avian brain to test a motor theory. The theory holds that vocal learning circuits evolved from motor circuits. The full text gives the brain maps across species. If language's roots are motor, bird brains offer the clearest living evidence of how the system was assembled.
plos-pone-0001868:
Simona Wagner, Chris J. Storbeck, Kristin Roovers, and their co-authors studied a kinase required for cell movement in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cell migration involves a host of signals that meet on the cell's internal frame, and it is needed for growth, immune defense, and tissue repair. Cells move by building and removing focal adhesions, the anchors that grip their surface.

Using knockdown and blocking tricks, the team shows the microtubule-associated Ste20-like kinase SLK is required for focal adhesion turnover. It acts under control of FAK and src family kinases. The full text gives the migration assays. Adhesion turnover is also the step wandering cancer cells exploit to spread.
plos-pone-0001968:
Caroline Esnault and co-authors measured how far two forms of the malaria mosquito have split, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The mosquito Anopheles gambiae, a main carrier of malaria in Africa, comes in two molecular forms, called M and S. Plans to release lab-made mosquitoes that cannot carry the parasite hinge on how freely the forms mix in the wild.

The team compared genes across the forms in Africa and found high genetic differentiation between them. A deep split means a released strain may stay in one form and not spread to the other. That fact shapes any plan to fight malaria by changing wild mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0002068:
Jules Beekwilder and co-authors asked what happens to pests when a plant loses its chemical shields, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Aliphatic glucosinolates are sulfur compounds found at high levels in Arabidopsis and kin plants of the cabbage family. When tissue is chewed, they break into biting products that resist pest insects.

The team used plants that lack these compounds and measured insect herbivory, the feeding damage done by insects. Past work showed the making of the compounds is governed by gene switches. Removing the shield tests how much protection it truly gives in practice, not just in the lab.
plos-pone-0002168:
Dongna Li, Hui Li, Caiying Ou, and co-authors traced the paternal lines of the native people of Hainan Island, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hainan sits at the southern entrance to East Asia, a crossroads where early migrations shaped the Y chromosome patterns of the whole region. The island's aboriginal groups have lived apart for a long time, which can preserve old genetic patterns.

By studying Y chromosome variation in these groups, the team assessed how isolated their gene pool is. They also used the data to infer what the region's early population structure looked like. Island peoples like these act as living records of how humans first spread through East Asia.
plos-pone-0002268:
Li-Qun Fang and co-authors mapped the environmental factors behind bird flu spread in mainland China, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Since late 2003, the highly pathogenic H5N1 virus had killed millions of poultry and tens of thousands of wild birds. By March 2008 it had also caused at least 373 confirmed human infections, of which 236 were fatal.

The team analyzed where outbreaks occurred and which features of the landscape went with them. Factors like water bodies, poultry density, and climate can flag high-risk areas in advance. Maps of risk help authorities aim surveillance and culling before the virus flares again.
plos-pone-0002368:
Caterina Hatzifoti, Andrew Bacon, Helen Marriott, and co-authors packaged a vaccine booster and its target together in fat bubbles, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Antibody against CD40 can strongly enhance vaccine responses when chemists link it to the vaccine antigen. That chemical linking step, though, creates production and quality control headaches, worse still when several antigens are combined.

The team instead packed the CD40 antibody inside liposomes along with bacterial sugar and protein antigens. The shared package induced enhanced IgG responses without chemical linking. A simpler way to get the boost could make combined vaccines easier to make and check.
plos-pone-0002468:
Research by Stahl and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from James E. Stahl, Jennifer E. Kreke, Fawaz Ali Abdul Malek, and others. Its subject is consequences of Cold-Ischemia Time on Primary Nonfunction and Patient and Graft Survival in Liver Transplantation: A Meta-Analysis. The ability to preserve organs prior to transplant is key to the organ allocation process.

The purpose of this study is to describe the functional relationship between cold-ischemia time (CIT) and primary nonfunction (PNF). What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002568:
Traka and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Maria Traka, Amy V. Gasper, Antonietta Melchini, and others. Its subject is broccoli Consumption Interacts with GSTM1 to Perturb Oncogenic Signalling Pathways in the Prostate. Past studies suggest that people who eat more than one portion of cruciferous vegetables per week face a lower risk of prostate cancer.

Yet the processes behind that link are still poorly understood, a gap the authors note at the start. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002668:

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Histone-modifying enzymes are essential for a wide variety of cellular processes dependent upon changes in gene expression. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002768:
Research from Julian W. Tang and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers seasonality of influenza A(H3N2) virus: a hong kong perspective (1997–2006). Authorship is credited in the record to Julian W. Tang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The underlying basis for the seasonality of influenza A viruses is still uncertain. The authors add a further point. Phylogenetic studies investigated this phenomenon but have lacked sequences from more subtropical and tropical regions, particularly from Southeast Asia. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002868:
Work by Pascal Vrtička and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with individual attachment style modulates human amygdala and striatum activation during social appraisal. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Pascal Vrtička, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Adult attachment style refers to individual personality traits that strongly influence emotional bonds and reactions to social partners. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002968:
Charles Chapple and Roderic Guigó tracked the loss of selenoproteins in insect genomes in 2008. Selenoproteins are a varied family built around selenocysteine, the twenty-first amino acid. Until recently, every animal genome checked had them, so they were thought essential for animal life.

Challenging that view, some insects had lost them. The authors argue that relaxed selective constraints let the losses happen independently in different insect lines. Published in PLOS ONE, the study shows even a once-universal protein family can be dropped when its benefits no longer outweigh its costs. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003068:
Takanari Inoue and Tobias Meyer used synthetic activation to find a logic switch for cell movement in 2008. The enzyme PI3K is widely studied as a principal regulator of cell polarization, migration, and chemotaxis. Surprisingly, neutrophils and Dictyostelium cells could still polarize and migrate in some studies without the usual inputs.

By switching on endogenous PI3K and Rac synthetically, the team identifies an AND-gate switch: both signals are needed together for polarization and migration. Published in PLOS ONE, a clear logic rule helps explain conflicting results in the cell movement field. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003168:
Ranjan K. Dash, Yanjun Li, Jaeyeon Kim and colleagues model energy use in muscle under low blood flow in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Control of cell metabolism and energy in skeletal muscle under stress, such as reduced blood flow and oxygen supply to mitochondria, can be understood in numbers with a multi-scale computer model. The team use such an integrated top-down model in in-silico studies.

Readers see how whole muscle behaviour and cell level processes can be linked in one framework. Models like this let researchers test stress responses that are hard to measure directly. They can also guide lab work by showing which measures matter most.
plos-pone-0003268:
Yasser EL-Manzalawy, Drena Dobbs and Vasant Honavar evaluate peptide prediction methods in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Choice of one method over another for MHC-II binding peptide prediction is typically based on published reports of estimated performance on standard benchmark datasets. The team show that several standard benchmark datasets of unique peptides used in such studies contain substantial overlap problems.

Readers learn that benchmark flaws can inflate how good prediction tools look. MHC-II binding prediction guides vaccine and immunology work, so honest benchmarks matter. The paper is a useful warning for any field that ranks algorithms on shared test sets.
plos-pone-0007468: To know whether an RNA virus is truly replicating, scientists must detect both strands of its genetic material — the genome and its mirror image. This study presents an accurate method for measuring each strand separately in infected cells and tissues. Better strand-specific counts let researchers follow the virus's life cycle step by step instead of guessing.
plos-pone-0007568: Conventional wisdom says never move animals into a declining population until you know why it is shrinking. Studying endangered brown bears, the researchers argue the rule can backfire when behavior or demographics — not habitat — drive the decline. The work offers a sharper framework for deciding when relocation can help recovery.
plos-pone-0007668: Strep throat's germ got a tiny-RNA sweep. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Perez's team swept group A streptococcus for small regulatory RNAs. The germ needs tight gene control to cause disease. The tiny-RNA list was built. The sweep feeds germ science.
plos-pone-0007768: A mutant RAS gene usually spells aggressive leukemia — but this study found a twist. In acute myeloid leukemia cells, oncogenic RAS made chemotherapy push the cells to mature rather than just die, via DNA damage and p53. The finding turns a feared mutation into a therapeutic lever.
plos-pone-0007868: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus causes gait problems, incontinence, and dementia in the elderly. This study characterized a new mouse model created with the mutagen ENU. The model gives researchers a way to study a disease with few good models.
plos-pone-0007968: Leaf shapes follow a global rule. This 2009 study proposed a global regulation that induces the shape of growing folded leaves. Rather than molecular blueprints alone, physics-style principles may govern how leaves unfurl into their final forms.
plos-pone-0008068: The genetics of inflammation was read pathway by pathway. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Eleftherohorinou and colleagues pooled genome-wide association results for three inflammatory diseases and asked which biological pathways carry the most risk variants. Single-gene hits had explained only a sliver of why these diseases run in families. By adding up small effects across each pathway, the team exposed the shared genetic burden. The pathway view points drug hunters toward biological processes rather than lone genes.
plos-pone-0008168: Histone messages end in a stem-loop, not a tail, and this study showed losing the processing factor SLBP causes genomic instability in flies. The finding ties proper histone production to genome integrity and cell proliferation.
plos-pone-0008268: A vitamin shortfall was tied to Parkinson-like damage. A 2009 PLOS ONE rat study by Orozco-Barrios's team broke B12 metabolism in the substantia nigra and watched neurons die. plos-pone-0008368: Cancer immune shots got a route rule. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Nierkens's team showed where CpG goes decides how well it fights tumors. Lab wins had not translated to clinics. The route rule was mapped. The rule feeds immunotherapy.
plos-pone-0008468: A sleeping-sickness germ's coat got a quality-control audit. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Field's team probed chaperone needs for building the trypanosome variant surface glycoprotein. plos-pone-0008568: Worm protein caretakers were found fading with age. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Kern's team showed HSF1-controlled chaperone capacity declines with age in worm neurons and muscle. plos-pone-0008668: Immune-cell maturation got marker flags. The sentinel cells' maturation stages needed labels. The marker set was decoded. The flags aid immune research.
plos-pone-0008768: Old wax-block tumors got a gene readout. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Beck's team built 3SEQ, a 3-prime sequencing trick for gene readouts from old archived tumor blocks. Formalin-fixed bits beat chip scans. The workaround was checked. The trick unlocks tissue banks.
plos-pone-0008868: Gut inflammation got a half-dose phosphatase test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Hassan's team showed mice with half TC-PTP develop worse DSS colitis. The immune enzyme's protective role was mapped. The test informs inflammatory bowel science.
plos-pone-0008968: Pig skin stem cells got a nerve-muscle makeover. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Lermen's team drove neuro-muscular differentiation of adult porcine skin-derived stem-like cells. The cross-lineage fate was confirmed. The makeover advances regenerative medicine.
plos-pone-0009168: An eye-disease gene's protein got a makeover map. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Ying's team charted posttranslational modifications, location, and partners of optineurin. The glaucoma gene's protein life was mapped. The map feeds eye-disease science.
plos-pone-0009268: Flu's surface spikes got a conserved-target hunt. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Sahini's team found conserved hemagglutinin regions for anti-viral targeting. The stable targets were mapped. The hunt feeds universal-flu-vaccine design.
plos-pone-0009368: Big-loss gamblers got a paradox read. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Takano's team found big losses push gamblers to wilder bets. The think-versus-impulse link was logged. The read feeds choice science. The bets grew after each loss.
plos-pone-0011468: Mitochondrial DNA mutator mice age in fast-forward, accumulating energy-factory errors. This research paper shows those mutations trigger mitochondrial failure, cell suicide, and sarcopenia — the wasting of skeletal muscle — in the animals' muscles. The chain of damage makes the mouse a vivid model of how mitochondrial decay may drive human aging.
plos-pone-0011568: Yeast cells relay mating and stress signals through a MAP kinase cascade, and the fidelity of that relay matters. This research paper measures the cascade's signal response sensitivity — how crisply output tracks input. The systems-level measurement reveals the design principles of a cellular telephone game.
plos-pone-0011668: Brain tumor cells divide relentlessly, and two accomplices — cathepsin B and uPAR — help them. This research paper depletes both in glioma cells and watches them stall in the G0/G1 resting phase via FOXO3a and p27. The double hit parks cancer cells in neutral, a promising brake.
plos-pone-0011768: Dogs suffer breast tumors too, and a chemical tweak called citrullination may be involved. This research paper asks whether the enzyme PAD2 drives that tweak on histone proteins in dog mammary cells. The canine angle tests a cancer mechanism across species lines.
plos-pone-0011868: Neurons fire spikes that start small in the cell body — but axons even them out. This research paper shows axons amplify incomplete somatic spikes into uniform amplitudes in mouse cortical neurons. The axonal evening reveals the wire as a signal shaper, not just a cable.
plos-pone-0011968: Caribbean reefs are missing their sharks — and humans are the reason. This research paper documents the large-scale absence of sharks on greater-Caribbean reefs as a footprint of human pressures. The missing-shark census indicts overfishing and finning worldwide.
plos-pone-0012068: Schizophrenia disrupts verbal working memory — and brain scans show how. This research paper uses event-related fMRI to study phonological verbal working memory in schizophrenia. The brain-scan patterns reveal the faulty circuitry behind the disorder in patients today and tomorrow.
